definition.text: An organized collection of data, usually managed by database management software that lets users and applications capture and analyze it.

facts.text: A database, the DBMS that manages it and the applications around it together form a database system, though people often use the word database loosely for any of the three.
Databases support the internal operations of organizations and underpin online interactions with customers and suppliers.
Examples include library systems, flight reservation systems, parts inventory systems and many content management systems that store websites as collections of webpages in a database.
Databases can be classified by the type of their contents, by their application area, or by a technical aspect such as the database structure or interface type.
An in-memory database lives primarily in main memory with non-volatile backup; it is faster than a disk database and used where response time is critical.
A distributed database is one in which both the data and the DBMS span multiple computers.

Storage redundancy improves performance and availability: materialized views store frequently needed query results, and replication keeps copies of database objects for simultaneous access and resilience to partial failure.
A backup, taken occasionally or continuously, keeps each desired database state in backup files so the database can be restored after corruption or erroneous updates.

definition.text: Software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to a database.

facts.text: The DBMS is the software between the database and its users or programs: it lets them capture, retrieve, update and analyze data, and it provides the facilities to administer the database, such as performance monitoring, tuning, and backup and recovery.
MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database and Microsoft Access are examples of DBMSs.
The core functionality of a DBMS is the storage, retrieval and update of data, but what a DBMS provides beyond that varies enormously.
Codd proposed that a general-purpose DBMS provide storage, retrieval and update, a metadata catalog, transactions and concurrency, recovery, authorization, remote access, and constraint enforcement.
The database engine is the core part of the DBMS that sits between the database and the application interface.
A general-purpose DBMS provides public APIs and optionally a processor for a database language such as SQL; a special-purpose DBMS may use a private API tied to a single application.
The acronym can name the database model: RDBMS for relational, OODBMS for object-oriented, ORDBMS for object-relational, and DDBMS for a distributed DBMS.

Client-server architecture put the application on a client and the database on a server so processing could be distributed; multitier architectures later added application and web servers, with the database connected only to the adjacent tier.

definition.text: A database model is a type of data model that determines the logical structure of a database and how its data can be stored, organized and manipulated.

facts.text: The most popular database model is the relational model, or its SQL approximation, which uses a table-based format.

Common logical data models include navigational, hierarchical, network, graph, relational, entity-relationship, object, document, entity-attribute-value and star schema models; an object-relational database combines the object and relational structures.
Other models include the inverted index (a physical data model) and the multidimensional, array and multivalue models.
Specialized models are optimized for particular types of data: XML, semantic, content store, event store and time series databases.
The flat model puts data in a single table, one record per row and one attribute per column; it is as simple as a spreadsheet but cannot efficiently handle complex relationships between entities.

The hierarchical model is a tree in which each record has one parent but can have many children; it suits clear parent-child relationships but struggles with many-to-many ones and can become complex and rigid.
The network model lets each record have multiple parents and children, forming a graph; it overcomes the hierarchical model's limits by handling many-to-many relationships efficiently.

definition.text: Special-purpose languages for working with a database, each specific to a particular data model.

facts.text: Database languages are split into sublanguages: data control (DCL) for access, data definition (DDL) for tables and relationships, data manipulation (DML) for inserting, updating and deleting, and data query (DQL) for searching.
SQL combines data definition, data manipulation and query in a single language and is supported, with varying conformance, by all mainstream commercial relational DBMSs.

A database language may also configure the DBMS, compute over query results (counting, summing, averaging, sorting, grouping), enforce constraints, and offer an API version of the query language for programmers.

definition.text: A unit of work performed in a database management system that is treated in a coherent and reliable way, independent of other transactions.

facts.text: Transactions serve two purposes: reliable units of work that allow correct recovery from failures and keep the database consistent, and isolation between programs accessing the database concurrently.
Without isolation between concurrent programs, their outcomes are possibly erroneous.
A bank transfer is one transaction: it requires subtracting the amount from one account and adding the same amount to the other.

A transaction must be atomic (complete or no effect), consistent (conform to existing constraints), isolated (not affect other transactions) and durable (written to persistent storage); these properties are abbreviated ACID.
A transactional database is a DBMS that provides the ACID properties for a bracketed set of operations (begin-commit), keeping the database consistent even under concurrent updates and failures.
The programmer sets a transaction's boundaries with special transaction commands, which define which code executions it includes.
A distributed transaction enforces the ACID properties over data on multiple nodes, and typically an entity coordinates the process so all parts are applied to all relevant systems.

Not every database supports ACID transactions, usually because it prioritizes optimizations that are hard or theoretically impossible to combine with them; relational databases usually support them and non-relational ones usually do not.

definition.text: The ACID property that determines how a transaction's changes are visible to other users and systems.

facts.text: A lower isolation level lets more users access the same data at once but increases concurrency effects such as dirty reads or lost updates.
A higher isolation level reduces the concurrency effects users may meet, but needs more system resources and raises the chance that one transaction blocks another.
Of the four ACID properties, isolation is the one most often relaxed.
To keep the highest isolation, a DBMS usually acquires locks on data, which can cost concurrency, or implements multiversion concurrency control.

Most transactions can be built to avoid high isolation levels such as SERIALIZABLE, which cuts locking overhead, but the programmer must analyze access code carefully because relaxed isolation can cause bugs that are hard to find.
Higher isolation levels make deadlock more likely, which also calls for careful analysis and programming techniques to avoid.
Isolation is typically enforced at the database level, though client-side systems such as a transaction manager can also provide global isolation and atomicity.
Full isolation lets a transaction run as if no others were running concurrently; this strictest form, serializability, is hard to implement in reality, so looser isolation levels are often adopted.

definition.text: Settings that control how much locking a transaction does when selecting data, trading protection from concurrency effects against concurrency.

facts.text: SERIALIZABLE guarantees the same effect as some serial execution, in which each transaction runs to completion before the next begins; lock-based systems hold read and write locks to the end and take range locks for ranged SELECTs.
Without locks, a serializable system detects write collisions among concurrent transactions and lets only one of them commit.
REPEATABLE READ keeps read and write locks until the end of the transaction but manages no range locks, so phantom reads can occur; write skew is possible in some systems.
READ COMMITTED guarantees that any data read was committed when read, but promises nothing if the read is repeated: data is free to change after it is read.
READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads, so one transaction may see not-yet-committed changes made by others.
Each level is stronger than those below it, so the standard lets a DBMS run a transaction at a stronger level than requested, for example Read committed performed as Repeatable read.
The default isolation level varies quite widely between DBMSs, and most transactional databases let the user set any level.
The ANSI definitions based on three read phenomena have been criticized as ambiguous and as not reflecting the isolation many databases actually provide.

title: Read phenomena in transactions

definition.text: The SQL-92 standard names three read phenomena that can occur when a transaction retrieves data another transaction might have updated.

facts.text: A dirty read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row that another transaction has updated but not yet committed; if that update is rolled back, the first transaction's view of the row is wrong.
A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row twice and another transaction commits an update to that row in between.
A phantom read occurs when a transaction retrieves a set of rows twice and another transaction commits an insert or removal in that set in between.
Dirty reads occur only at READ UNCOMMITTED, non-repeatable reads at READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED, and phantom reads at every level except SERIALIZABLE.
Write skew lets two writers who each read the same columns both update them, leaving data that mixes the two transactions; it is possible at REPEATABLE READ in some systems.
Being free of all three phenomena is necessary but not sufficient for a serializable schedule.
A serialization anomaly is a fourth phenomenon: the result of committing a group of transactions is inconsistent with every possible ordering of running them one at a time.
The SQL standard only specifies which phenomena must not occur at each level, so a database may give stronger guarantees; PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read, for example, allows no phantom reads.

definition.text: The mechanisms in a DBMS that handle isolation and guarantee the correctness of concurrent transactions.

facts.text: Concurrency control constrains the timing of data access operations to orders that have the serializability and recoverability properties, which typically reduces performance.
Serializability is often compromised for better performance when correctness allows, but recoverability cannot be compromised because that typically violates database integrity.

Two-phase locking is the most common concurrency control method in DBMSs: a transaction must first acquire a lock on an object, and acquiring it may be blocked while another transaction holds a lock on it.

Many databases rely on locking to provide ACID: the transaction marks the data it accesses, even data only read, so others cannot modify it until it ends; non-trivial transactions need many locks, causing overhead and blocking.

definition.text: A database based on the relational model, which stores data in tables of rows and columns.

facts.text: A relational model organizes data into tables of columns and rows with a unique key identifying each row, and many relational systems let users query and update with SQL.
Each table generally represents one entity type, such as customer or product; its rows are instances of that type and its columns hold values attributed to each instance, such as address or price.

The model supports data integrity and avoids redundancy through keys and normalization, handles many-to-many relationships, supports complex queries and transactions, and is queried with the simple language SQL.
To operate efficiently and accurately, a relational DBMS must use ACID transactions.
No commercial implementation conforms to all of Codd's 12 rules, so the term relational has come to describe a broader class of database systems.

The relational database became the predominant type, replacing hierarchical and network databases because it was easier to implement and administer; NoSQL databases are now a popular alternative thanks to horizontal scaling of computer clusters.
Singh lists relational databases' advantages as simple and accurate, accessible, consistent and flexible.
Singh lists their disadvantages as expense to maintain, difficult schema evolution, performance hits from joins and denormalization, and difficult scaling because of poor horizontal scalability.

definition.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table, and a foreign key is a column that holds the key of a row in another table to link them.

facts.text: Most implementations give every row a unique primary key; a new unique value is generated when a row is written, the system uses it primarily to access the table, and system performance is optimized for it.

A surrogate key is an artificial attribute with no intrinsic meaning that uniquely identifies an object, such as a student ID; natural attributes are sometimes good primary keys, but surrogate keys are often used instead.
Natural keys can be defined as alternate keys, but they often need several columns, called a composite key; this is one reason a single integer column is usually made the primary key.
A foreign key is a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table; when a primary key migrates to another table it becomes a foreign key there, and foreign keys need not be unique.
A foreign key restricts the values of an attribute in the referencing table to values that exist in the referenced table, which is how tables are cross-referenced.

Migrating a primary key into another table represents a one-to-one or one-to-many relationship; most designs resolve many-to-many relationships with an extra table that holds the primary keys of both entity tables.

definition.text: Rules that restrict the data that can be stored in the relations of a database.

facts.text: Constraints are usually expressions that return true or false for whether the data satisfies them, and they can apply to a single attribute, to a tuple, or to an entire relation.
A domain is the set of possible values for an attribute and acts as a constraint on it: the string "ABC" is not in the integer domain but 123 is.
Constraints can restrict a domain further, such as limiting an integer attribute to values between 1 and 10, and they implement business rules in the database; SQL does this with check constraints.
The two principal rules of the relational model are entity integrity and referential integrity.

definition.text: Executable code that is associated with, and generally stored in, the database.

facts.text: Stored procedures collect and customize common operations, such as inserting a tuple into a relation, gathering usage statistics, or encapsulating complex business logic and calculations.
Procedures can greatly reduce the information transferred within and outside a system, and access can be granted only to the stored procedures and not directly to the tables for added security.
Stored procedures are not part of the relational model, but all commercial implementations include them, often with vendor-specific procedural extensions to the declarative SQL syntax.

definition.text: The operations of relational algebra, such as selection, projection and join, that express queries against a relational database.

facts.text: Queries on a relational database are expressed in relational calculus or relational algebra; in his original algebra Codd introduced eight operators in two groups of four.

Four operators come from set theory: union (SQL UNION), intersection (INTERSECT), set difference (EXCEPT or MINUS) and the cartesian product, which matches every tuple of one relation with every tuple of the other (CROSS JOIN).
The other four are selection (SELECT with a WHERE clause), projection (extracting only specified attributes), join (connecting relations by their common attributes) and division.
In SQL an INNER JOIN prevents a cartesian product, so a query over N tables needs N-1 inner joins.

definition.text: A definition of the shape of a data structure that specifies what kinds of data can go where.

facts.text: A schema can be strictly enforced across the entire database, loosely enforced on part of it, or not exist at all.
A table has columns like a spreadsheet, from two to a hundred or more; a column holds values of one type, such as text, numbers, enums or timestamps, with one value per row.
Data in a table is recorded in rows, and a table can hold thousands or millions of rows.
In SQL every record conforms to a fixed schema whose columns are chosen before data entry and changed later only through migrations; in NoSQL the schema is dynamic and fields can be added on the fly.

title: Views and materialized views

definition.text: A view is a relation computed from other relations by relational operations rather than one that stores data.

facts.text: Relations that store data are called base relations, and in implementations they are called tables.
Derived relations store no data but are computed by applying relational operations to other relations; in implementations they are called views or queries.
A materialized view is a pre-computed data set derived from a query and stored for later use, so querying it is faster than querying the base table, significantly so for frequent or complex queries.
Materialized views also enable data subsetting, which reduces network loads, and are mostly used for performance and replication.

title: OLTP and OLAP

definition.text: OLTP systems serve transaction-oriented applications and respond to users in real time, while OLAP systems answer complex analytical queries for reporting and decision support.

facts.text: OLTP serves transaction-oriented applications such as order entry, retail sales, financial transactions and ATMs; it suits systems needing strong consistency, and operational databases process relatively high volumes of updates using transactions.
OLTP applications have high throughput, are insert- or update-intensive and serve hundreds of concurrent users; their key goals are availability, speed, concurrency and recoverability (durability).
OLTP is concerned with concurrency and atomicity: concurrency control stops two users modifying the same data at once, and atomicity makes all steps of a transaction succeed together or all fail.

OLAP answers multi-dimensional analytical queries for business intelligence or reporting; compared with OLTP, its queries are much more complex and run in smaller volumes, and it is optimized for complex queries and data analysis.
OLTP handles all query types (read, insert, update, delete), whereas OLAP is generally optimized for read-only operations.

OLTP databases hold detailed, current data in normalized entity schemas, usually third normal form; OLAP databases store aggregated, historical data in multi-dimensional schemas, usually star schemas.

Operational (loosely OLTP) databases benefit from row-oriented DBMSs, while analytics (loosely OLAP) databases benefit from column-oriented ones, because analytic access usually selects specific fields rather than whole rows.
OLTP performance is measured in transactions per second; OLAP is characterized by a low rate of transactions and complex queries with aggregations, and its performance measure is response time.

title: Star and snowflake schemas

definition.text: A star schema is the simplest data warehouse schema: a central fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive attributes; a snowflake schema normalizes those dimension tables.

facts.text: The star schema is the simplest data mart schema style and the most widely used for warehouses: fact tables reference any number of dimension tables, and the shape gives the name, with the fact table at the center.

Facts hold measurable, quantitative data such as sales price, quantity, distance or weight; dimensions hold descriptive attributes such as product models, colors, sizes, locations and salesperson names.

Fact tables record metrics for specific events as numeric values plus foreign keys to dimensions, at a low uniform grain, so they accumulate many rows; types are transaction, snapshot and accumulating snapshot.
Dimension tables have relatively few records but many attributes each, commonly time, geography, product, employee and range, and carry a surrogate primary key mapped to the natural key.
Star schemas are denormalized: relaxing normalization gives simpler join logic and reporting, faster read-only queries and aggregations, fewer joins per query, and an efficient source for OLAP cubes.

A snowflake schema normalizes dimension hierarchies into multiple linked tables, reducing redundancy and improving integrity but needing more joins; it suits large or frequently updated dimensions, and Kimball advises avoiding it without clear need.

Analytic queries over a star schema usually join one large fact table with a handful of small dimensions, a pattern many DBMSs optimize with star-join; a sales example joins Fact_Sales to Dim_Date, Dim_Store and Dim_Product.
Dimensions with only a few attributes are simpler to maintain but force queries with many table joins, making the schema harder to use.

definition.text: Pick the kind of database that matches the workload: transactional, analytical, text search, document, key-value, graph, vector or geospatial.

facts.text: OLTP databases suit transactional systems requiring strong consistency, and OLAP databases are optimized for complex queries and data analysis.
Full-text search databases give fast, flexible text search; document stores hold and query JSON-like documents; key-value stores offer high-speed, simple data models.
Graph databases manage highly connected data, embedding databases store and retrieve vector representations efficiently, and geospatial databases specialize in location-based data and queries.
Singh advises weighing both the ACID and BASE models and the application's own requirements when choosing a database.

title: Multiversion concurrency control

definition.text: A non-locking concurrency control method that keeps multiple versions of each data item so readers see a consistent snapshot while writers write.

facts.text: Locks make readers wait for writers and cause contention, especially between long read transactions and update transactions; MVCC avoids this by keeping multiple copies of each data item.
An update creates a newer version instead of overwriting, so each user sees a snapshot of the database at one instant and a writer's changes stay invisible to others until it commits.
The version a transaction sees depends on the isolation level; the most common with MVCC is snapshot isolation, where a transaction observes the data as of when it started.
Readers pick the version by timestamp or transaction ID, so reads and writes are isolated without locks and writers do not block readers, though some MVCC databases such as Oracle still use locks.

In a timestamp scheme each version has read and write timestamps; a transaction reads the latest version preceding its timestamp, and a write by a transaction older than the object's read timestamp is aborted and restarted.

In one worked example each row has hidden transaction_id and roll_pointer columns, a write adds a new row pointing back to the old one, and a transaction's Read View fixed at its start keeps returning balance 100.

Obsolete versions need cleanup: some systems sweep and rewrite the table periodically, as PostgreSQL's VACUUM FREEZE does, while others keep the latest version plus an undo log, which can run out of space and abort transactions.
The drawback is the cost of storing multiple versions; the benefit is that reads are never blocked, which matters for read-heavy workloads.

definition.text: A set of four properties of database transactions, atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, intended to guarantee data validity despite errors, power failures and other mishaps.

facts.text: Relational databases follow the ACID properties to maintain data integrity before and after a transaction.
Atomicity means all or nothing: the writes in a transaction are executed all at once and cannot be broken into smaller parts, and if a fault occurs they are rolled back.

Consistency means preserving database invariants: data written by a transaction must be valid under all defined rules. This differs from consistency in the CAP theorem, where every read receives the most recent write or an error.

Isolation keeps concurrent transactions from contending; the database moderates access so transactions appear to run sequentially, and the strictest form, serializability, makes each act as if it were the only one running.
Durability means data stays persisted after a transaction commits, written to disk, even through a system failure; in a distributed system this means the data is replicated to other nodes.

Implementations use write-ahead logging, which writes the prospective change to a persistent log before changing the database so it can recover after a crash, or shadow paging, which applies updates to a partial copy activated on commit.

Guaranteeing ACID across a distributed database is harder because a network connection or another node may fail; the two-phase commit protocol provides atomicity by having a coordinator ask participants if they are prepared before formalizing the transaction.

definition.text: A looser alternative to ACID, built on basic availability, soft state and eventual consistency, that NoSQL databases often adopt to gain scale and resilience.

facts.text: BASE properties are much looser than ACID guarantees, and there is no direct one-for-one mapping between the two models.
In the NoSQL world ACID transactions are less common, because some databases loosen requirements for immediate consistency, data freshness and accuracy in order to gain scale and resilience.
Basic availability means the database appears to work most of the time; soft state means stores need not be write-consistent nor replicas mutually consistent all the time.
With eventual consistency, data may not be consistent immediately but eventually becomes consistent; reads remain possible but may give an incorrect response in the meantime.
To scale and stay highly available, the logic moves from the database to separate servers, so the database becomes more independent and focused on storing data.

title: ACID vs BASE

definition.text: The choice between strict ACID transactions and looser BASE guarantees depends on the application's requirements.

facts.text: Singh says there is no right answer: both models were designed to satisfy different requirements, so choosing a database means weighing both models against the application's needs.
A fully ACID database is the perfect fit for use cases where data reliability and consistency are essential.
Given BASE's loose consistency, developers must be more rigorous about consistent data and must know the chosen database's BASE behavior and work within its constraints.
Planning around BASE limitations can be a major disadvantage compared with the simplicity of ACID transactions.

Databases built around traditional ACID guarantees, such as RDBMS, choose consistency over availability, while BASE systems common in NoSQL choose availability over consistency; MongoDB and Redis keep consistency and compromise availability on a network partition.

An ACID database fails the whole transaction if any step errors; a BASE database lets users read inconsistent data temporarily and reaches consistency later. A database leans toward one or the other, though some NoSQL databases show certain ACID traits.
SQL databases such as MySQL and PostgreSQL are structured over the ACID model, while NoSQL databases such as DynamoDB or ElasticSearch use the BASE architecture.

contested_note: Singh presents ACID and BASE as fitting different requirements, with no single right answer.

definition.text: A type of database design, named for "not only SQL" or "non-relational", that stores and retrieves data differently from the table-based structure of relational databases.

facts.text: Rather than rows and columns, a NoSQL database holds information in a single data structure such as key-value pairs, wide columns, graphs or documents; without a fixed schema it scales easily to large, often unstructured datasets.

NoSQL systems are sometimes called "Not only SQL" because they can support SQL-like query languages or work alongside SQL databases in polyglot-persistent setups, where multiple database types are combined.

NoSQL databases are popular in big data and real-time web applications for their simple design, horizontal scaling across clusters of machines and precise control over data availability; cheap commodity hardware can host them.

Many NoSQL systems follow the BASE model, prioritizing speed and availability over strict consistency (per the CAP theorem) through eventual consistency: updates reach all nodes eventually, but reads may be stale.
Most NoSQL systems lack full ACID transaction support, sacrificing it for performance and scalability, though some, like MongoDB, include it as a key feature.
Barriers to adoption include low-level query languages instead of SQL, no ad hoc joins across tables, no standardized interfaces and large existing investments in relational databases.

NoSQL databases are classified by data model, mainly key-value, document, wide-column and graph, plus time-series databases for time-stamped data and multi-model databases that combine several models in one backend.
NewSQL is a class of modern relational databases that aims to give NoSQL-like scalable performance for read-write online transaction processing while still using SQL and keeping ACID guarantees.

title: Document database

definition.text: A database designed to store, retrieve and manage documents, or semi-structured information, and one of the main categories of NoSQL databases.

facts.text: A document is a self-contained unit encoding data in a standard format such as XML, YAML, JSON or binary BSON, and corresponds to an object in programming; the store is made for documents rather than tables.
Documents need no fixed schema: documents in one collection may have different fields, unlike rows of a table, so new information can be added to some documents without affecting others.
Each document is addressed by a unique identifier, often a string, URI or path, and most stores index that key to speed retrieval.

Beyond key access, an API or query language retrieves documents by content or metadata, such as all documents whose field matches a value; features vary by product, and an update can replace a whole document or single fields.

Key-value stores treat values as opaque, while document stores exploit internal structure: a query can find phone numbers containing 555 without matching postal code 55555; for simple needs the difference can be minimal.

Relational databases split one object across tables joined by foreign keys; a document database keeps everything about an object in one document fetched by key without multi-table lookups, which also avoids object-relational mapping.

Singh lists intuitive and flexible, easy horizontal scaling and schemaless as advantages, schemaless and non-relational as disadvantages, and calls document databases general-purpose for transactional and analytical applications.

title: Key-value store

definition.text: A data store for storing, retrieving and managing associative arrays (dictionaries), in which each record is stored and found through a unique key.

facts.text: The associative array (map or dictionary) is its data model: a collection of key-value pairs in which each key appears at most once; it is one of the simplest non-trivial models, and richer ones often extend it.

The value is opaque to the database, which typically supports only storing, retrieving, updating and deleting a value by its key; a document store can interpret record structure, a key-value store returns a value whole.

This suits low-latency, high-throughput workloads of direct key lookups, and Singh lists simple, performant, highly scalable, optimized lookups and session management as strengths; it is less suited to complex queries or relationships.

Limits: basic CRUD, values that cannot be filtered, no indexing or scanning, no optimization for complex queries; lack of standardization and limited transaction support long confined many systems to specialized uses.

Variants add structure: keys can be kept in lexicographic order so key ranges are retrieved efficiently, keys can be composite with major and minor parts, and some stores support complex values such as Redis lists.
Consistency ranges from eventual to serializable and is sometimes configurable against latency and availability; data may live in memory, on solid-state drives or on rotating disks.
In-memory examples include Memcached and Redis; persistent ones include Berkeley DB, Riak and Voldemort, and RocksDB is a persistent key-value storage engine developed at Facebook.

title: Graph database

definition.text: A database that uses graph structures to represent and store data, with nodes for entities, edges for the relationships between them, and properties.

facts.text: Relationships are first-class: edges can be labeled, directed and given properties, and linking data items directly means they can often be retrieved with one operation.

Most use index-free adjacency, with nodes holding direct references to neighbors instead of a global index; adjacent lookups are typically O(1) versus O(log n) for an index, so query time tracks the part of the graph touched.

In the labeled-property graph model, nodes and relationships are named, carry key-value properties, and edges are directed; in RDF, each added piece of information is a separate statement of subject node, predicate arc and object node.
They handle graph-like queries naturally, such as shortest path, diameter and community detection, and new data can be added to an existing graph without planning every future use case.

Relational databases need many joins over several tables for complex relationships; a graph database follows stored links and avoids costly joins, and its advantage grows with query depth and complexity.

Relational systems suit flat data with relationships one or two levels deep and are typically faster at one operation over many elements; the graph model alone should not justify replacing a relational database without evidence of gains.

Suited to social relations, transport links, road maps and network topologies; Singh lists fraud detection, recommendation engines, social networks and network mapping, and a social network's friends relationship is essentially unbounded.
As of 2021 no graph query language had been universally adopted as SQL was; multi-vendor options include Gremlin, SPARQL and Cypher, and ISO's GQL is meant to be a declarative standard like SQL.

title: Wide-column store

definition.text: A type of NoSQL database that uses tables, rows and columns but lets column names and formats vary from row to row, storing columns in column families.

facts.text: It can be read as a two-dimensional key-value store: each value is identified by two keys, a row identifier and a column identifier.

Columns are grouped into column families stored together on disk, inside a top-level keyspace; a row can span several families, a family is often likened to a relational table, and supercolumns nest a map of other columns.

The name once meant column-oriented relational databases like C-Store but came to mean Bigtable, Apache Cassandra and similar systems that keep column families together and drop the relational model; Bigtable is the prototypical example.

Compared with relational databases they are denormalized, with columns added dynamically and rows of varying columns; compared with document databases, records are split into column families the database treats as units, not whole documents.

Singh calls them highly scalable, able to handle petabytes and ideal for real-time big data applications, lists increased write time as a disadvantage, and names business analytics and attribute-based data storage as uses.

notes: replaces the earlier thin entry built on Singh bullets; article moved to the Wikipedia page

definition.text: A performance problem where code runs one query plus N additional queries to fetch data that a single query could have returned.

facts.text: It happens when the data access layer executes N additional SQL statements to fetch the same data that could have been retrieved by the primary SQL query.
The larger the value of N, the more queries are executed and the larger the performance impact.
It is commonly seen in GraphQL and ORM tools, and is addressed by optimizing the SQL query or using a dataloader that batches consecutive requests into a single data request.

title: SQL vs NoSQL databases

definition.text: The two main kinds of database, SQL (relational) and NoSQL (non-relational), differ in how they are built, what they store and how they store it.

facts.text: Relational databases are structured with predefined schemas, while non-relational ones are unstructured, distributed and have a dynamic schema; SQL stores data in tables of entities and data points, NoSQL in models such as key-value, graph or document.
In SQL each record has a fixed schema chosen before data entry and changed only through migrations; in NoSQL the schema is dynamic, fields are added on the fly and a record need not have every field.
SQL is a very powerful language for defining and manipulating data; NoSQL queries are focused on a collection of documents, and the syntax differs between databases.

SQL databases usually scale vertically, which can get very expensive, and scaling across servers is challenging; NoSQL databases scale horizontally on cheap commodity hardware, and many distribute data across servers automatically.

The vast majority of relational databases are ACID compliant, so for data reliability and safe transactions SQL is still the better bet; most NoSQL solutions sacrifice ACID compliance for performance and scalability.
Reasons to pick SQL: structured data with a strict schema, relational data, a need for complex joins, transactions, and very fast lookups by index.
Reasons to pick NoSQL: a dynamic or flexible schema, non-relational data, no need for complex joins, a very data-intensive workload, and very high throughput for IOPS.
Singh says to pick the technology that fits the requirements better, and warns that claiming NoSQL is simply better or SQL is not scalable reflects poorly in an interview.

contested_note: Singh treats SQL and NoSQL as a trade-off to settle by requirements, not as a contest with a single winner.
notes: the 'for SQL' and 'for NoSQL' reason lists are grouped by the source's list order; the group labels are not sentences in the dossier

definition.text: The states a transaction passes through, from active to committed, or failed and aborted, until it is terminated.

facts.text: A transaction starts in the active state, where it is being executed; when it executes its final operation it is partially committed, and when all operations succeed it is committed and its effects are permanently established.

A transaction is failed if any check by the recovery system fails, and cannot proceed; the recovery manager then rolls back all its writes to restore the database to its state before the transaction, and the transaction is aborted.
After an abort the recovery module can restart or kill the transaction; with no rollback, or after a commit, the system is consistent and ready for a new transaction and the old one is terminated.

definition.text: A domain-specific language used to manage data, especially in a relational database management system.

facts.text: SQL is a set-based, declarative language, not an imperative one like C or BASIC, designed to query data in a relational database; extensions add procedural features such as control-of-flow constructs.
Its two advantages over older read-write APIs such as ISAM or VSAM were accessing many records with one single command and not having to specify how to reach a record, with or without an index.

Statements fall into sublanguages for data query (DQL), data definition (DDL), data control (DCL) and data manipulation (DML), covering querying, insert, update and delete, schema creation and modification, and access control.

SQL was among the first commercial languages to use Codd's relational model; it became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987, and despite departing from the model it became the most widely used database language.

Virtually no implementation adheres fully to the standard, so most SQL code needs changes to port between systems; the standard is large and complex and leaves behavior such as indices and file storage to implementations.
Date and time syntax, string concatenation, NULLs and comparison case sensitivity vary from vendor to vendor.

SQL deviates from the relational model: tables and query results are lists of rows, so a row may repeat and row order can be used in queries, which a primary key or unique constraint avoids for duplicates.
The Null marker indicates the absence of a value, distinct from 0 for an integer or an empty string for text, and it enforces three-valued logic of true, false and unknown.

definition.text: Because most NoSQL databases cannot join in queries, related data is handled by multiple queries, by storing copies of values, or by nesting data.

facts.text: Since most NoSQL databases cannot join data in queries, the schema generally needs to be designed differently; there are three main techniques for handling relational data.
Multiple queries: instead of one query, run several; NoSQL queries are often faster than SQL queries so the cost may be acceptable, but if too many are needed another approach is more appropriate.
Non-normalized data: instead of storing only foreign keys, store the actual foreign values with the data, such as a username in each blog comment, so no further lookup is needed.
Copied values must be changed in many places when they change, such as a username, so this approach works better when reads are much more common than writes.
Nesting data: in document databases like MongoDB, put more data in fewer collections, such as blog comments inside the post document, so one retrieval returns all the data a task needs.

title: Querying and indexing in NoSQL
article: NoSQL#Query optimization and indexing in NoSQL databases

definition.text: How NoSQL databases handle queries on fields that are not indexed, and what indexing features they offer to speed them up.

facts.text: Many NoSQL databases perform full-table or collection scans for queries on non-indexed fields, applying filters after retrieving the data; DynamoDB, MongoDB, Cassandra, Couchbase, HBase and Redis behave differently here.

Modern NoSQL databases add optimizations: MongoDB supports compound indexes, Cassandra offers secondary indexes and materialized views, Redis uses custom indexing, and Elasticsearch uses inverted indexes for text search but can still scan non-indexed fields.

Many NoSQL systems are designed for scalability and efficient key-based operations rather than arbitrary-field queries, so they excel at basic CRUD and key lookups, while suitability for complex queries or joins varies by database type and implementation.

definition.text: A class of relational database systems that seek the scalability of NoSQL systems for online transaction processing while keeping the ACID guarantees of a traditional database.

facts.text: Financial and order-processing systems outgrew conventional relational databases but needed transactional guarantees NoSQL could not give; the old options were bigger computers or custom distribution middleware, both costly, and NewSQL tries to reconcile this.
The two common distinguishing features are the online scalability of NoSQL systems and the relational data model, including ACID consistency, with SQL as the primary interface.

Typical applications have heavy OLTP volumes of short-lived transactions that touch little data and use a small number of query forms; some systems also support hybrid transactional/analytical processing (HTAP).

Systems fall into three groups: shared-nothing clusters where each node manages a subset of the data, optimized storage engines behind a SQL interface, and transparent sharding across nodes using Raft or Paxos consensus.

definition.text: Using multiple data storage technologies within a single system to meet varying data storage needs.

facts.text: The idea mirrors polyglot programming: as the right language for each job may beat one language for everything, an application can talk to several databases and use each for what it does best.
Forcing one database to satisfy every requirement can yield a non-performant jack-of-all-trades, master-of-none solution, because different databases solve different problems.

Joins enforce relationships in a relational database but become problematic as data grows; a graph database may handle relationships at scale but not transactions, which relational systems serve better; a document database can hold the unstructured part.
Martin Fowler expects any decent-sized enterprise to use varied storage technologies for different kinds of data, first asking how the data will be manipulated and only then choosing the technology.
Knitting several database products together has two major drawbacks: a significant increase in operational complexity, and no support for keeping data consistent across the separate stores.

definition.text: A pessimistic concurrency control method that guarantees conflict-serializability by making each transaction acquire all its locks before releasing any.

facts.text: The protocol uses locks that a transaction applies to data and that may block other transactions from accessing the same data during the transaction's life.

Locks are acquired in an expanding phase with none released, then released in a shrinking phase with none acquired; a transaction never acquires a lock after releasing one, and schedules obeying this are serializable.

The basic protocol uses shared (read) and exclusive (write) locks: reading needs a read or write lock, writing needs a write lock, and several locks on one object may coexist only if none is a write lock.
Because locks block, two-phase locking and its strict variants can deadlock when two or more transactions block each other.

Strict 2PL releases write locks only after the transaction commits or aborts, which gives strictness; strong strict 2PL also holds read locks until the end, so the transaction has only a growing phase until it completes.
In practice most commercial database systems use strong strict two-phase locking, which ensures global serializability if all participating databases use it.

Conservative 2PL takes every lock before execution so a lock holder never blocks; it shortens lock holding under heavy contention but over-locks under light contention and needs declared read and write sets, so it is rarely used.
Two-phase locking is a concurrency control protocol and should not be confused with the two-phase commit protocol.

title: Snapshot isolation

definition.text: A guarantee that all reads in a transaction see a consistent snapshot of the database and that the transaction commits only if its updates do not conflict with concurrent updates made since that snapshot.

facts.text: A transaction works on a personal snapshot taken when it starts and commits only if the values it updated have not been changed externally since; such a write-write conflict aborts it.

It is usually implemented within multiversion concurrency control, which keeps versions of each item; the transaction need only store its list of updates, which is scanned for conflicts before commit.

Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and MongoDB, among others, adopted it because it performs better than serializability while still avoiding most, but not all, of the anomalies serializability avoids.

It is not serializable: it shows none of the anomalies the ANSI SQL-92 standard prohibited, yet permits others such as write skew, which is why it was used to criticize that standard's isolation levels.
The naming is confusing: Oracle, and PostgreSQL before 9.1, call snapshot isolation their serializable mode, so users must know the difference to avoid anomalous behavior.

The 1995 paper critiquing ANSI SQL isolation levels shows that dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms fail to characterize several popular isolation levels, introduces new phenomena, and defines Snapshot Isolation as an important multiversion isolation type.

PostgreSQL implements Repeatable Read with snapshot isolation: a query sees a snapshot as of the start of the transaction's first non-transaction-control statement, so successive SELECTs see the same data.
Some systems offer Repeatable Read and Snapshot Isolation as distinct levels with different behavior, whose permitted phenomena researchers formalized only after the SQL standard was written.

title: Write skew

definition.text: An anomaly in which two concurrent transactions read an overlapping data set, make disjoint updates and both commit, neither having seen the other's update.

facts.text: Under serializability write skew is impossible, because one of the two transactions would have to occur first and be visible to the other; snapshot isolation permits it.

Example: a bank lets either of two accounts run a deficit if their total stays at or above zero; two concurrent $200 withdrawals each check against their own snapshot, both commit, and the total ends at -$200.
The fix is to force a write-write conflict: add a conflict table both transactions update, or promote a read to a write, such as Oracle's SELECT FOR UPDATE or rewriting a value with itself.

The workarounds have costs: a table that materializes the constraint violates normal form, promotion is not always possible, and snapshot isolation leaves the user to maintain non-trivial constraints.

Serializable Snapshot Isolation detects and aborts dangerous triplets of concurrent transactions (shown by Cahill et al. in 2008), removing the workarounds at the cost of more aborts; PostgreSQL 9.1 adopted it.

definition.text: An approach to quickly answering multi-dimensional analytical queries, part of business intelligence, in which users analyze data organized in cubes interactively.

facts.text: Typical uses are business reporting for sales and marketing, budgeting, forecasting and financial reporting; OLAP tools let users analyze multidimensional data interactively from several perspectives.
At its core is the OLAP cube: numeric facts called measures, categorized by dimensions, placed at the intersections of a hypercube and usually manipulated through a pivot-table-like interface.
Cube metadata is typically built from a star or snowflake schema in a relational database: measures come from fact table records and dimensions from the dimension tables.

Three basic operations: roll-up aggregates along dimensions (offices up to a division), drill-down navigates into detail (sales by product within a region), and slicing and dicing takes a subset of the cube and views it along other dimensions.

Aggregations, built from the fact table by coarsening granularity along dimensions, are the main reason OLAP is fast; it has been claimed that cubes answer complex queries in around 0.1% of the time needed on OLTP relational data.

Because the number of possible aggregations is huge, usually only a predetermined number are fully calculated and the rest solved on demand; choosing which is the view selection problem, which is NP-complete.
COUNT, MAX, MIN and SUM can be computed per cell then combined in a roll-up, and AVERAGE needs a sum and a count; DISTINCT COUNT, MEDIAN and MODE need the whole set and are hard to do efficiently.

title: MOLAP, ROLAP and HOLAP

definition.text: OLAP systems are traditionally grouped by storage into multidimensional (MOLAP), relational (ROLAP) and hybrid (HOLAP) types.

facts.text: MOLAP, the classic form of OLAP, stores data in an optimized multi-dimensional array rather than a relational database, and often precomputes derived data such as consolidations into a data cube.

ROLAP works directly with relational databases and needs no precomputation: base and dimension tables are relational tables, new tables hold the aggregates, and it depends on a specialized schema design.
ROLAP scales better to large volumes and very high-cardinality dimensions and works with any SQL reporting tool, but it is generally slower than MOLAP and aggregate tables need custom ETL code.

MOLAP generally delivers better performance and needs less storage thanks to specialized indexing and compression, but can suffer database explosion from many dimensions, precomputed results and sparse data.

Most commercial OLAP tools now use Hybrid OLAP, letting the designer choose what sits in MOLAP and what in ROLAP: aggregations in MOLAP and detail in ROLAP, or recent data in MOLAP and older data in ROLAP.

contested_note: Vendors disagree about the specifics of each type's benefits.
notes: Wikipedia flags the benefit comparison as contested (S:b796e08bd4f6)

definition.text: A central repository of data integrated from disparate sources and organized for reporting and analysis, used by analysts and managers to make decisions.

facts.text: Data from operational systems such as marketing or sales is uploaded, often cleansed first, through extract-transform-load (ETL) or extract-load-transform (ELT) workflows; the warehouse stores current and historical data organized for analysis and reporting.

Operational databases are normalized to protect integrity and record transactions fast, spreading one transaction over dozens to hundreds of tables, with quick inserts and updates and periodic purging of older data.

Warehouses are optimized for analytic access that selects specific fields, so they suit column-oriented storage while operational databases favor row-oriented DBMSs; operational systems keep a snapshot of the business, warehouses keep history.

Analysis on a separate copy relieves the lock contention long-running analysis queries cause in transaction processing databases, keeps history the source systems may not, and integrates many sources into one data model.
Warehouse data is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and nonvolatile: it spans a long horizon (up to 10 years) and is read-only once loaded, unless a regulatory obligation requires change.

The two main storage approaches are dimensional (Kimball), using star schemas that split data into facts and dimensions for easier understanding and faster retrieval, and normalized (Inmon), storing third-normal-form tables grouped by subject area.

A data mart is a simple warehouse for one subject area, often built by one department; bottom-up design builds marts first and integrates them, top-down design builds a normalized warehouse and derives dimensional marts.
A data lake instead keeps large volumes of data raw, in structured, semi-structured and unstructured form, processed at run time, which suits machine learning and big data processing.

definition.text: Two workflows for loading a data warehouse: ETL transforms data before loading it, while ELT loads raw data into the warehouse and transforms it there.

facts.text: An ETL warehouse uses staging, integration and access layers: staging holds raw data extracted from each source, and the integration layer transforms it, often into an operational data store.

Integrated data then moves into the warehouse database, arranged into dimensions, facts and aggregate facts, and the access layer helps users retrieve it; ETL is inherently a batch process in most implementations.

ELT drops the separate transformation tool: data is extracted from heterogeneous sources and loaded straight into a staging area inside the warehouse, where all transformations run before landing in target tables.

definition.text: A database optimized for time series data, a sequence of data points indexed in chronological order.

facts.text: Early time series databases were data historians recording sensor measurements; today they also serve infrastructure and application monitoring, IoT telemetry, smart energy grids and financial tick data.

The data is uniform, timestamps mapped to metric values, and grows rapidly; entries rarely need cross-table relationships, so relational constraints are skipped, and workloads seldom need indefinite retention, which cuts storage and speeds queries.

They exploit sequential uniformity with specialized compression such as delta encoding or Gorilla compression, temporal indexing, and lifecycle management that downsamples or drops whole old partitions in bulk.

Built for append-only, high-velocity ingestion, they aim for write throughput, low-latency range queries, compression and multi-window aggregation; many tag points with key-value metadata or device IDs to query by time interval and source.

definition.text: A database management system designed to support multiple data models against a single, integrated backend.

facts.text: Most DBMSs are organized around one data model; a multi-model database stores, indexes and queries data in more than one, such as document, graph, relational and key-value.

It answers polyglot persistence, whose several products bring significant operational complexity and no consistency across stores, by offering the modeling advantages of many models in a single data store.

Reported advantages over single-model databases include ingesting varied formats such as CSV and JSON without extra effort, one query language such as AQL or SQL/JSON over related data, and multi-model ACID transactions in stand-alone mode.
Architectures differ: some engines support models such as documents and graphs natively, while others provide each model as a separate layer on top of an engine such as a key-value store.

definition.text: A vector database stores and retrieves embeddings of data in vector space; it is also called a vector store or vector search engine.

facts.text: Embeddings are machine-learned vectors in a space of a few hundred to tens of thousands of dimensions, so that semantically similar items, whether words, documents, images or audio, get vectors close to each other.

Vector databases typically use approximate nearest neighbor algorithms to find records semantically similar to an input, unlike traditional databases that look up records by exact match; uses include semantic search and recommendation engines.

Common techniques for similarity search on high-dimensional vectors include Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs and locality-sensitive hashing, which may be combined; HNSW-based implementations have been among the best performers in recent benchmarks.

In retrieval-augmented generation, document embeddings are stored with a link to the document; the prompt's embedding queries the database for relevant documents, which are added to the language model's context window.

title: Elasticsearch

definition.text: A distributed, open search and analytics engine, built on Apache Lucene, for storing, searching and analyzing large volumes of data quickly.

facts.text: Traditional databases are sometimes not fast enough to store, search and analyze huge volumes of data in near real time with results in milliseconds; Elasticsearch addresses this.
Elasticsearch is a distributed search engine for textual, numerical, geospatial, structured and unstructured data, built on Apache Lucene, with an HTTP web interface and schema-free JSON documents.
Documents are stored in indices divided into primary shards, each with zero or more replicas distributed across cluster nodes; routing and rebalancing are handled automatically.
Once an index has been created, the number of primary shards cannot be changed.
It supports full-text search, faceted search, real-time search, multitenancy and percolation, in which stored queries are matched against incoming documents rather than the reverse.
Real-time GET requests make it usable as a NoSQL datastore, though it does not support distributed transactions.
Geo data is supported by geo_point fields for lat/lon pairs and geo_shape fields for points, lines, circles and polygons.

In the primer's design the Lucene search cluster is scatter-gathered: every server is asked for matches, then results are merged, ranked, sorted and returned, with tweets kept in memory to keep latency low.

definition.text: A spatial database is a general-purpose database, usually relational, enhanced with spatial data that represents objects in a geometric space, along with tools for querying and analyzing it.

facts.text: Most spatial databases represent points, lines and polygons, and their data types are mostly based on the OGC Simple Features specification.
A spatial extension adds spatial datatypes that store spatial data as column values; because locations need a spatial reference system, the database also tracks and transforms coordinate systems.

It also adds spatial functions to the query language, in most relational systems as functions in SQL SELECT statements; the OGC standard specifies measurement, geoprocessing, predicate, geometry-constructor and observer operations.

A spatial join of cities and countries is an SQL query such as SELECT * FROM cities, countries WHERE ST_Contains(countries.shape, cities.shape); predicates answer true or false questions such as whether two polygons overlap.
Ordinary indexes sort values in a linear order, which is not optimal for queries in two or three dimensions, so spatial databases use a spatial index designed for multi-dimensional ordering.
The R-tree is typically the preferred spatial index: it groups objects by minimum bounding rectangle and adds each object to the rectangle whose size increases least.
Almost all current relational and object-relational DBMSs have spatial extensions, while some NoSQL systems such as MongoDB and CouchDB support only simplified or modified sets of the operations.
Web mapping applications need spatial databases whenever they handle dynamic data that changes frequently or a huge amount of geographic data.

definition.text: A connection pool is a cache of reusable database connections managed by the client or middleware.

facts.text: Pooling reduces the overhead of opening and closing connections, improving performance and scalability in database applications.

SQL databases typically use stateful binary protocols that keep session information such as transaction states and prepared statements, so pooling matters; DynamoDB and Cosmos DB use stateless HTTP-based protocols, which often reduces the need.
Pool settings should match the database's capacity and the workload; overprovisioned pools cause rejected connections, throttling, resource contention and higher latency.

Idle pooled connections can break through NAT timeouts, dropped connections or session invalidation, and expired authentication tokens can invalidate connections in the pool, forcing costly reconnection.
In serverless setups AWS Lambda opens a new database connection per invocation, which can cause connection storms under high concurrency; a proxy such as Amazon RDS Proxy pools the connections.

Containers hold database connections for their lifecycle and virtual machines scale connection demand with instance count, so without a pooler such as HikariCP or pgbouncer idle or excessive connections strain the database.
Pooling is usually done on the client side, by libraries such as ADO.NET and JDBC or by database SDKs, not by the database engine.
A web crawler service can improve performance by keeping many open connections at a time, which is called connection pooling.

definition.text: PostgreSQL accepts the four standard transaction isolation levels but implements three distinct ones, built on its multiversion concurrency control.

facts.text: PostgreSQL's Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed, because that is the only sensible way to map the standard levels onto its multiversion concurrency control architecture.
Read Committed is the default: a SELECT sees only data committed before the query began, so two successive SELECTs in one transaction can see different data if others commit between them.

In Read Committed a would-be updater of a row another transaction is changing waits for it to commit or roll back; if it committed, the WHERE clause is re-evaluated on the updated row before proceeding.

Read Committed is fine for simple cases such as transferring $100 between accounts, but unsuitable for complex search conditions, because one command can see an inconsistent snapshot of rows touched by concurrent commands.
Repeatable Read sees only data committed before the transaction began; this is stronger than the standard requires, preventing every phenomenon except serialization anomalies, phantom reads included.

A Repeatable Read transaction that tries to modify a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction is rolled back with a serialization failure, so applications must retry the whole transaction; read-only transactions never conflict.

Repeatable Read gives a stable view, but not necessarily one consistent with a serial execution: a read-only transaction may see a control record updated but miss a detail record, so business rules need explicit locks.
Sequence changes are immediately visible to all other transactions and are not rolled back when the transaction that made them aborts.
